# Can an Illinois Association Fine an Owner? Notice and Hearing

CenterPoint Association Management Published October 26, 2026 6 min read

Every board eventually faces an owner who will not stop: the dog on the roof deck, the contractor working at 7 a.m. on a Sunday, the balcony grill the insurance carrier flagged. Letters do not work, and someone asks whether the association can simply start fining. In Illinois the answer is yes, but the statute attaches a condition that boards skip more often than any other: notice and an opportunity to be heard, before the fine.

## Does Illinois law allow a condo board to fine an owner?
Yes. Section 18.4(l) of the Condominium Property Act gives the board power, after notice and an opportunity to be heard, to levy reasonable fines for violations of the declaration, bylaws, and rules and regulations of the association. The power is real, but the procedure comes first and the amount must be reasonable. A fine imposed without that process is exposed to challenge.

The same subsection also lets the board impose charges for late payment of assessments. Late charges and fines are different tools: a late charge responds to non-payment, while a fine responds to a violation of the documents and carries the notice-and-hearing requirement.

Our [rule enforcement service](https://www.centerpointmgmt.com/services/violation-management) builds this notice-and-hearing process into every enforcement case.

## Is the rule the same for an HOA?
Substantially, yes. For communities governed by the Common Interest Community Association Act, Section 1-30(g) gives the board power, after notice and an opportunity to be heard, to levy and collect reasonable fines from members or unit owners for violations of the declaration, bylaws, operating agreement, and rules and regulations. The wording tracks the condominium statute closely.

One caveat for smaller HOAs: under CICAA Section 1-75(a), an association organized under the General Not For Profit Corporation Act with 10 units or fewer, or annual budgeted assessments of $100,000 or less, is exempt from CICAA unless its directors or members vote to be covered. An exempt association should ask counsel what fining authority its own documents provide.

## What counts as notice and an opportunity to be heard?
The statutes do not define a specific form of notice, a deadline for responding, or a hearing format. Those details come from your declaration, bylaws and adopted rules, and from what a court would consider fair. Because the statute is silent, boards should have counsel review a written enforcement procedure before relying on it, rather than improvising one case at a time.

In practice, a defensible procedure usually includes:

- A written notice identifying the specific provision violated, what happened, and when.
- The fine that may be imposed, and whether it repeats for continuing violations.
- A date, time and place where the owner can appear before the board, or a way to respond in writing.
- A reasonable amount of time between the notice and the hearing.
- A written decision sent after the hearing.

None of those elements is a specific statutory number. They are the components that make it easy to show, later, that the owner actually had notice and a real chance to respond.

## Can the hearing be held in closed session?
The discussion can be. Section 18(a)(9)(A)(iv) allows a condominium board to close a portion of a noticed meeting to discuss violations of the association's rules and regulations, and CICAA Section 1-40(b)(5)(iv) says the same for HOAs. But both statutes require that any vote on those matters take place at a meeting, or portion of one, that is open to owners. The decision to impose a fine is a vote, so it belongs in open session, even if the facts were discussed privately. Many boards record the decision by unit number rather than owner name.

## What makes a fine reasonable?
Neither statute sets a dollar cap or a schedule, so we will not suggest one. What the statutes require is that fines be reasonable. Boards are in a stronger position when the amounts are set in advance in an adopted fine schedule, applied consistently to every owner, and proportionate to the violation. A fine schedule is a rule, so in a condominium it is adopted through the Section 18.4(h) process: a meeting of the unit owners called for the specific purpose of discussing the proposed rules, with the full text included in the notice.

Consistency is the part boards underestimate. A fine against one owner for a violation the board has ignored in five other units invites a selective-enforcement argument. Before the first notice goes out, check whether the rule has actually been enforced.

## Do the governing documents still matter?
Yes. The statutes grant the power and set the minimum procedure; your declaration and bylaws may add steps, such as a required warning letter, a specific hearing panel, or a minimum response period. Where the documents add requirements, follow them. Where they conflict with the Act, the Act controls. Section 18 also requires that condominium bylaws contain restrictions designed to prevent unreasonable interference with other owners' use of their units and the common elements, and a method for adopting and amending rules (Section 18(k) and (l)).

## What if the owner disputes the facts at the hearing?
Then the hearing is doing its job. The purpose of an opportunity to be heard is that the board might change its mind, so treat the owner's account as evidence rather than as an obstacle. If the owner produces something new, such as a contractor's permit, a photo with a different date, or a statement that the noise came from another unit, the board can postpone the decision, ask the manager to verify, and decide at the next open meeting.

Boards get into trouble when the hearing is a formality and the decision was obviously made beforehand. Directors who have already told neighbours the owner will be fined should consider whether they can listen fairly. Where a director has a personal dispute with the owner, stepping back from that vote is the cleaner course.

Whatever the board decides, write it down: what the owner said, what the board considered, and why it reached its result. A short written decision is far easier to defend than a recollection.

## A fining checklist for Illinois boards

- **Confirm the rule exists and was properly adopted.** You cannot fine for violating a rule that was never adopted through the required process.
- **Confirm the fine schedule** is adopted and that the amount is in it.
- **Document the violation** with dates, photos where appropriate, and the provision broken.
- **Send written notice** naming the violation, the possible fine, and how and when the owner can be heard.
- **Hold the hearing.** Listen, take notes, and let the owner finish. Discussion can be in closed session.
- **Vote in open session** and record the decision in the minutes.
- **Send the written decision** and post the fine to the owner's ledger only after the vote.
- **Apply the same steps to the next owner,** including board members.

## When should the board call counsel instead?
Call counsel before fining if the owner has asserted a disability-related accommodation, if the violation involves religious items (Section 18.4(h) bars rules that prohibit reasonable accommodation for religious practices), if fines have been accruing for months without a hearing, or if the board intends to pursue collection of fines in court. How fines can be collected and secured is fact-specific, and boards should not assume fines are treated the same as unpaid assessments.

Fining well is mostly paperwork done in the right order.
